title: Price a cable reel

blocks.text: GridCap's undergrounding crews pull cable from standard reels of `reel` metres, cut into pieces of a few standard lengths; the season needs $`d_k`$ pieces of length $`\ell_k`$. A column generation master chooses how many reels to cut with each pattern, and after each master solve its cover rows' duals price one piece of each length. The pricing problem asks for the pattern, the pieces cut from one reel, worth the most at those prices.

Write the pricing problem first: its variables with domains and bounds, its objective, and its row with a label. Then write `best_reel(prices, pieces, reel)` to solve it without a solver, and return `(value, pattern)`: the pattern's worth at the prices and the pattern itself, a dict from piece name to count (counts of zero left out). `pieces[name]` is `(length, demand)`; lengths and `reel` are whole metres. On small reels the tests compare your value with every pattern tried by brute force. One test prices a 1,000-metre reel with eight lengths and up to 30 pieces of each: that is $`31^8`$ count combinations, too many to try one by one, so it stops your function after 10 seconds. Trying every pattern is not the method this practice asks for.
About twelve lines; dynamic programming over metres used is one way.

cases.says: at the master's prices, the reel is cut into the pieces worth the most that fit its length
pieces may fill the reel exactly, with no metre left over
a pattern never cuts more pieces of a length than the season's jobs need
a 1,000-metre reel with eight lengths is priced in seconds, which trying every pattern cannot do

origin.section: The Master's Duals Price Each Task, and the Pricing Problem Finds the Best New Day

concepts: the pricing problem finds the pattern worth most at the master's duals
